query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, the synergy between mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperature arises because wear continuously removes protective oxide and passivation layers while exposing heterogeneous phases that differ in corrosion resistance. This results in micro‐galvanic cells along interphase boundaries (e.g., between the mechanically robust BCC matrix and the more corrosion‐sensitive Laves or secondary phases), thereby accelerating both wear and corrosion beyond the sum of their individual effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a dominant BCC phase and secondary phases (e.g., Laves phases) at well‐defined phase boundaries, as produced by methods such as spark plasma sintering.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous mechanical wear and a corrosive environment at elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., in the range 1200–1400 °C as in comparable studies) and an aggressive corrosive medium (such as an acidic or oxidizing solution) applied concurrently with mechanical wear.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries and microstructural heterogeneities that facilitate local galvanic coupling between phases with differing redox stability.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically erodes the protective oxide layers that normally impede corrosion, preferentially exposing regions (especially at phase boundaries) that are more susceptible to corrosion due to galvanic coupling. This localized corrosion further weakens the interphase bonds and roughens the surface, thereby exacerbating wear. The interplay between these processes accelerates the overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline with either isolated wear or isolated corrosion, the combined exposure will lead to a significantly higher total material degradation. Both wear scar depth and corrosion pit density/depth are expected to increase, indicating that each mechanism is amplified by the presence of the other. Exact quantitative changes remain uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and test conditions.
generation.baseline: A matched set of tests where samples are exposed separately to only wear or only corrosion under the same elevated temperature and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys under elevated temperature conditions in corrosive media where distinct phases with different corrosion resistances are present. It may not apply to single-phase alloys or to conditions where protective scales fully regenerate between wear events.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the accelerated degradation and the relative contribution of wear versus corrosion are uncertain; further experimental quantification is needed to refine these estimates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three groups of samples: one subjected solely to mechanical wear under elevated temperature, one exposed only to the corrosive medium at the same temperature, and one exposed to both wear and corrosion simultaneously. All tests should be performed on the same multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with identical initial microstructures. The wear component can be applied using a standardized sliding or abrasive setup, and corrosion monitored via electrochemical means.
measurements: Microstructural analysis at phase boundaries (pre- and post-test)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation (as measured by mass loss, wear scar metrics, and corrosion pit parameters) under simultaneous wear and corrosion is not statistically significantly greater than the sum of the individual effects observed in the wear-only and corrosion-only tests, then the proposed mechanistic explanation based on synergistic removal of protective oxides and interphase galvanic activity would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
